query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that integrates high-throughput DFT with machine learning uncertainty quantification can accurately identify single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys exhibiting lattice thermal conductivities at least 20–30% lower than those predicted by conventional DFT models. This improvement arises because the approach explicitly accounts for enhanced force-constant fluctuations and lattice distortions inherent to high configurational entropy, which are not fully captured by traditional methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeNiCu) synthesized with minimal secondary phases and characterized to have a uniform disordered solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Application of a predictive screening method that combines high-throughput DFT calculations with an ML algorithm trained on descriptors of local chemical disorder (e.g., mixing entropy, atomic radius variance) and force-constant fluctuations.
generation.conditions: Simulations carried out at room temperature with subsequent experimental validation under controlled conditions (e.g., laser flash thermal diffusivity measurements and inelastic neutron scattering for phonon dispersion) in samples processed to maintain a single-phase microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortions and localized force-constant fluctuations induced by multi-principal element mixing, leading to reduced phonon mean free paths.
generation.mechanism: The approach works by accurately capturing the distribution of local chemical environments and the resulting variations in interatomic force constants, which increase phonon scattering rates. This mechanism reduces the lattice thermal conductivity compared to predictions from models neglecting such disorder.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive method will identify candidate HEA compositions that, when synthesized, exhibit measured lattice thermal conductivities at least 20–30% lower than those estimated by conventional predictive models. For example, if traditional DFT predicts a conductivity of 5 W/(m·K), the new approach would identify compositions achieving values around 3.5–4 W/(m·K).
generation.baseline: Predictions from standard DFT calculations that do not incorporate detailed ML-based uncertainty quantification and local disorder descriptors.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be applicable only to single-phase, fully disordered high-entropy alloys with high configurational mixing; it may not extend accurately to multiphase systems or compounds with significant secondary phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties stem from the training dataset’s representativeness, approximations in the DFT calculations for disordered systems, and potential deviations in experimentally synthesized microstructures from idealized models.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the predicted low-thermal-conductivity HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeNiCu) using standard casting methods to ensure a single-phase microstructure. Measure its lattice thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis and assess phonon dispersion via inelastic neutron scattering. Compare the experimental values with the outputs of both the new predictive approach and conventional DFT predictions.
measurements: Laser flash thermal diffusivity (to determine lattice thermal conductivity)
Inelastic neutron/X-ray scattering (to quantify phonon mean free paths and dispersion)
Microstructural analysis (XRD, TEM) to confirm single-phase structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity of the synthesized HEA deviates by more than ±10% from the predictions of the integrated DFT-ML approach (and does not show the anticipated 20–30% improvement over conventional predictions), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained. papers.title: Rare‐Earth‐Zirconate Porous High‐Entropy Ceramics with Unique Pore Structures for Thermal Insulating Applications
papers.approach: Experimental fabrication using a TBA‐based gel‐casting method to tailor pore structures and multi‐element compositions
papers.findings: Ceramics with high porosity (67–81%) showed ultra‐low thermal conductivity at room temperature (0.064–0.121 W/(m·K)) and maintained insulation performance under high-temperature flame exposure; compressive strength was also competitive.
papers.mechanism: The high-entropy effect induces severe lattice distortions, while the tailored dual (micron‐sized) porosity provides complementary phonon scattering; together they reduce the phonon mean free path.

papers.title: Phonon behavior in a random solid solution: a lattice dynamics study on the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi
papers.approach: Combination of inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering experiments with lattice dynamics simulations
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits acoustic phonon dispersions throughout the Brillouin zone with force-constant fluctuations estimated between 20–50%; surprisingly, the phonon contributions to thermal conductivity were similar to those in simpler binary alloys.
papers.mechanism: Strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations that enhance phonon attenuation while preserving long-range order, yielding a balance between disorder-induced scattering and crystalline vibration modes.

papers.title: Dual-Porosity (Ta₀.₂Nb₀.₂Ti₀.₂Zr₀.₂Hf₀.₂)C High-Entropy Ceramics with High Compressive Strength
papers.system: TaNbTiZrHfC high-entropy ceramics with dual porosity
papers.approach: Pressureless sintering with a mixture of ceramic precursor and SiO₂ microspheres to generate both fine and larger pores
papers.findings: The ceramics achieved exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivity (as low as ~0.5–2.8 W/(m·K) depending on porosity) while also exhibiting high compressive strength; the dual-porosity structure was found to be competitive with traditional ultra-high-temperature ceramics.
papers.mechanism: Severe lattice distortions from multiple principal elements coupled with dual-size porosity enhance phonon scattering (both at the atomic level and at pore interfaces), significantly reducing thermal transport.

papers.title: Investigation of PbSnTeSe High-Entropy Thermoelectric Alloy: A DFT Approach
papers.approach: First-principles density-functional theory integrated with Boltzmann transport theory and on-the-fly machine-learned force fields
papers.findings: The calculated lattice thermal conductivity is very low (below 0.4 W/(m·K)), and the study provides a full suite of transport coefficients; for n-type doping, thermoelectric performance is enhanced.
papers.mechanism: Lattice distortion from multi-principal element alloying reduces phonon velocity and increases scattering, resulting in a significant drop in lattice thermal conductivity.

papers.title: Exploring thermophysical properties of CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy via molecular dynamics simulations
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations to study the effects of chemical composition, system size, and temperature on lattice thermal conductivity
papers.findings: Lattice thermal conductivity (kₚ) increases with system size; temperature and chemical composition significantly affect kₚ, providing insight into size effects and scaling for nanoscale to macroscale predictions
papers.mechanism: Intrinsic atomic-level disorder from multiple principal elements leads to enhanced anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions and scattering that limit phonon mean free paths.

established: High-entropy systems (both alloys and ceramics) exhibit low lattice thermal conductivity primarily due to severe lattice distortions and enhanced phonon scattering caused by chemical disorder and force-constant fluctuations.
Dual mechanisms—atomic-level disorder and engineered pore structures—can synergistically reduce thermal conductivity in materials designed for thermal insulation.

Experimental measurements (inelastic scattering, thermal diffusivity tests) and simulations (DFT, MD) consistently show that increasing compositional complexity leads to reduced phonon mean free paths.

approaches_tried.approach: Experimental fabrication of porous high-entropy ceramics (e.g., rare-earth zirconates, TaNbTiZrHfC) using gel casting and pressureless sintering
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved low thermal conductivity and maintained mechanical stability suitable for high-temperature insulation

approaches_tried.approach: DFT and Boltzmann transport-based predictions (integrated with machine learning force fields)
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided accurate predictions of ultra-low lattice thermal conductivity (<0.4 W/(m·K)) in selected high-entropy thermoelectric alloys

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations to probe size, temperature, and compositional effects on kₚ
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed systematic trends that help scale nanoscale predictions to macroscopic behavior

mechanisms: Lattice distortion and severe force-constant fluctuations due to multi-principal element mixing increase phonon scattering.
Dual pore structures introduce additional interfacial scattering, effectively reducing phonon mean free paths.
Enhanced anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions in disordered systems further lower phonon velocities.
disagreements: Some lattice dynamics studies (e.g., on FeCoCrMnNi) observe that increasing the number of elements does not proportionally increase phonon attenuation as predicted by simple theories (e.g., Mu’s theory), leading to debates on quantitative estimates of force-constant fluctuations.
There is differing emphasis on the contributions of intrinsic (atomic-level disorder) versus extrinsic (engineered porosity) factors in reducing thermal conductivity.
open_questions: How broadly applicable are predictive models (DFT/ML, MD) across the vast compositional space of high-entropy alloys for thermal-insulation purposes?
What is the quantitative threshold of lattice distortion or pore size/distribution needed to achieve a target ultralow thermal conductivity?
How do electronic contributions (if any) and phonon scattering mechanisms interplay in different classes of high-entropy systems under varied temperature regimes?
opportunities: Combine high-throughput DFT/ML or KKR-CPA based screening with targeted MD simulations to predict low-thermal-conductivity HEAs not yet synthesized.
Design experiments that precisely control both the compositional complexity and pore architecture to decouple intrinsic versus extrinsic phonon scattering mechanisms.

Establish a decisive experimental benchmark by measuring acoustic phonon dispersion and directly quantifying the phonon mean free path in a predicted HEA; a failure to observe the predicted reduction would falsify the hypothesis.

directions.direction: Integrate high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations with machine learning (ML) algorithms to predict lattice thermal conductivity by explicitly accounting for force‐constant fluctuations from high configurational entropy.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the prediction of low phonon thermal conductivity by capturing atomic-level disorder. It is strongly supported by evidence that high-entropy alloys exhibit severe lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations (see record IDs PMC9726824::web::014::discussion and PMC9822225::web::004::1_introduction). The physics is well established and the integration of DFT with ML has shown promise in similar high-throughput screenings. It is feasible with current computational resources, and its predictions can be tested against measured phonon spectra and thermal conductivity.

directions.direction: Develop a predictive model based on kinetic Monte Carlo simulations and molecular dynamics that directly simulate phonon transport in chemically disordered HEAs, then compare predicted mean free paths to experimental inelastic scattering measurements.
directions.assessment: This method combines simulation of phonon dynamics with experimental benchmark data (e.g., via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering as in PMC9726824::web::010::individual_acoustic_phonon_properties). It directly addresses the phonon-mean-free-path reduction mechanism but is computationally intensive and sensitive to the simulation cell size, which may limit its wide applicability.

directions.direction: Design controlled synthesis experiments to produce single-phase, fully disordered HEAs and systematically vary compositional parameters, then correlate experimentally measured thermal conductivity (via laser flash analysis) with predictions from the new predictive approach.
directions.assessment: This experimental route would enable a direct test of the predictive approach by correlating synthetic control with measured performance. It respects constraints related to maintaining phase purity and is supported by tailoring studies in high-entropy ceramics (e.g., PMC10143762::web::023::3_results_and_discussion). However, the large compositional space and microstructure control issues might complicate the interpretation.

directions.direction: Implement a data-driven screening framework that uses descriptors capturing local chemical disorder (such as mixing entropy, atomic radius variance, and bond strength distributions) to rank candidate HEA compositions for low thermal conductivity.
directions.assessment: This approach leverages statistical learning from existing data on HEAs (supported by multiple reports including PMC9822225::web::004::1_introduction) and could reduce the search space efficiently. The method’s accuracy depends on the quality and diversity of the training data, and its applicability may be limited to well-characterized systems.

directions.direction: Apply controlled thermomechanical treatments to modify defect densities in HEAs and use subsequent inelastic scattering experiments to assess the changes in phonon scattering rates, comparing these with predictions from the new approach.
directions.type: Heat or thermomechanical treatment with characterization
directions.assessment: This experimental intervention addresses extrinsic factors affecting phonon transport and can help decouple intrinsic atomic-level disorder effects from processing-induced defects. Although it respects the need to correlate structure with thermal properties, it is less direct in testing a predictive algorithm’s validity.

choice.direction: Integrate high-throughput DFT calculations with machine learning algorithms to predict lattice thermal conductivity by explicitly accounting for force‐constant fluctuations from high configurational entropy.
choice.why: This direction directly addresses the core limitation by capturing the atomistic origins of enhanced phonon scattering in HEAs. It builds on well-established physical principles and prior evidence (e.g., severe lattice distortions in HEAs, see PMC9726824::web::014::discussion and PMC9822225::web::004::1_introduction) and provides a computational framework that can be decisively benchmarked against precise experimental measurements of phonon dispersion and thermal conductivity.
